title: Small-business profitability, revenue, and employment paths diverge by firm size
source_unit: Federal Reserve Banks Small Business Credit Survey employer firm

denominator.unit: employer-firm respondents in the 2024 Small Business Credit Survey; 3,935 had 1–9 employees

profitability_diffusion.unit: percentage-point diffusion index: percent at a profit minus percent at a loss

observations.method: Weighted Small Business Credit Survey estimate for employer firms; profitability question refers to the end of the year before the survey year.
observations.uncertainty: The SBCS is a non-random survey of firms contacted directly or through community organizations, weighted by industry, location, and demographics. The profitability observation is retrospective and its reference year differs from other survey questions.
observations.subgroup: All employer firms and firms with 1–9 employees; additional size comparison includes firms with 10 or more employees.
observations.counterinterpretation: Improved reported profitability can coexist with weak revenue growth, owner compensation changes, lower costs, or changed firm composition; a diffusion index is not a profit margin.

denominator.unit: employer-firm respondents reporting next-12-month revenue expectations in the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey; 4,036 had 1–9 employees

revenue_past_12_months.value: more respondents reported lower than higher revenue; the smallest firms drove the lower-revenue result

revenue_expectation_change.unit: percentage-point year-over-year change in the share of firms expecting higher revenue in 2026

smallest_firm_pricing_power.unit: reported comparative pricing and sales pattern

observations.method: Weighted SBCS responses from employer firms; past-12-month revenue and next-12-month expectations are separate questions with separate valid universes.
observations.uncertainty: The reported direction and expectation change do not identify realized revenue, prices, quantities, or demand for a particular firm. Survey branching and non-random recruitment remain relevant.
observations.subgroup: All employer firms, firms with 1–9 employees, and firms with 10 or more employees.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower revenue expectations may reflect macro forecasts, sector mix, local demand, input costs, or respondent sentiment; lower pricing power does not by itself establish customer benefit or firm distress.

denominator.unit: employer-firm respondents reporting past-12-month employment change; 4,004 had 1–9 employees

small_firm_employment_growth.unit: reported direction of employment diffusion index in 2025

large_firm_employment_growth.value: decreased year over year while remaining positive
large_firm_employment_growth.unit: reported direction of employment diffusion index in 2025

credit_constraint.value: lower share received less than full financing requested and higher share reported no need to apply

observations.method: Weighted SBCS employer-firm responses, with debt-per-employee calculated as average total debt outstanding divided by employees.
observations.uncertainty: Employment growth and debt are firm-level reported indicators; they do not show worker pay, hours, job quality, household spillovers, or whether credit was affordable. Question-specific valid samples differ.
observations.subgroup: Firm size, especially 1–9 employees versus 10 or more employees.
observations.counterinterpretation: Small-firm employment growth can coexist with falling revenue or lower wages; lower reported credit constraint can reflect lower demand for credit rather than abundant affordable credit.

April 2026 national EHI report and SBCS charts.

boundary: This record measures weighted employer-firm survey indicators for profitability, revenue, employment, financing, debt, pricing, and technology/supply-chain challenges. It does not establish firm survival, local service access, worker household outcomes, customer prices, market power, or political action. The SBCS is non-random and question universes vary.
